# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

The last plate was cleared and his mother had begun to stack them by habit, the rhythm of any ordinary evening, when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] looked up from the table and asked the question plainly.

"Can I climb the hill again soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father set down his glass and considered this not as a breach but as a reasonable request from a boy who had climbed a hill and lived to ask for another morning. His mother's hand paused on the table. Marcos, still in the corner chair, did not move.

"Yes," his father said. "The same rule holds."

This was exactly the answer [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had hoped for and somehow did not expect. He felt something settle in his chest—not the hammering anticipation that had driven him up the hill four days ago, but something quieter: the knowledge that the world was larger than he had believed, and that he could move through it again.

Before he could speak further, there was a sound at the gate—a small, polite knock. It was Rosa, flour dust still on her sleeves though the bakery had closed hours ago. She stood in the kitchen doorway with the air of someone who had been waiting and had finally decided on courage.

"[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]?" she said, her words tumbling out quickly. "My mother said you would tell me everything about the other side, and I said you would not dare to, and then I said I would come and make you, and I have been at the gate since supper started because I was nervous about interrupting, but now I am here." She stopped for breath. "Can I come next time? When you climb again? I promise I am not afraid of the dark—well, I am, but only a small amount, and I can carry things."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] felt Bruno shift against his leg, tail thumping softly. He looked at Rosa's determined face and understood that she had been waiting not to hear the story, but to be asked into the next one.

"Yes," he said. "Come with us."

His mother smiled in the way that suggested this was exactly what she had meant when she said he would want to tell Rosa everything. Marcos tapped his walking stick once against the floor—not twice, not yet—and his eyes moved between the two children with an expression of quiet approval.

It was only after Rosa had been sent home with a promise to prepare supplies and a piece of his mother's bread that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] remembered the other thing, the thing he had been turning over in his mind since he woke this morning.

He thought of Elena in her yard on the far side of the hill, bent over the earth looking for what it had left behind. He thought of showing her the wooden treehouse observatory that he and Marcos had built together, the one that smelled of dust and pencil marks and time. He thought of her climbing the wooden ladder nailed into the fig tree and seeing the lens polished by his own hands, the cardboard telescope, the boards he had labeled with stars—and then he remembered the truth of it, the rule that lived inside it.

He looked at Marcos.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud, the way a question should be asked.

The kitchen was still. His mother's hands were quiet on a bowl. His father was watching. Bruno's ears pricked forward, attentive to the tone of something important being said.

Marcos set down his walking stick and tapped it twice against the stone floor.

Tap. Tap.

The sound of truth about to be spoken.

"Yes," Marcos said, his voice steady and thin as old paper. "It is half hers now, too."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] understood this was not quite what the rule said, but it was what the rule meant. The observatory belonged to him and to Marcos in equal measure, and now Marcos was saying yes, plainly, in one sentence, because this was an answer that could be carried. It meant that when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed the hill again with Rosa, when they reached the far side and found Elena, he could bring her back across and up the wooden ladder into the space that smelled of stars and dust and the work of their own hands.

The evening was cooling toward its end. The light had taken on the quality it always did near sunset—neither truly gold nor truly orange, but something between that made ordinary things look like they were being remembered rather than seen. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Marcos walked together through the house, through the garden where the olive trees cast their long shadows, to the fig tree with its wooden ladder and the treehouse observatory perched in the branches like a bird's careful nest.

Bruno preceded them, his tail high, no tension in his body now—only the simple certainty of a dog who knew his person was safe and his place was beside him.

Marcos climbed first, his movements slow and deliberate, his walking stick left below. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] followed, feeling the wooden rungs solid beneath his feet, a ladder built by his grandfather's hands and his own patience. The treehouse creaked the way it always did, and that sound was home now, was proof of making something that lasted.

Inside, the space was smaller than the sky it held. The window Marcos had scavenged fitted perfectly, and through it the emerging stars were beginning to appear like small, patient lights. The cardboard telescope stood in its place. The boards around the walls were still marked with [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s pencil labeling: Polaris, Altair, the shape of Cassiopeia he had traced and retraced until he could see it without looking.

Together, without speaking, they climbed to the high shelf where light fell clearest and longest. Marcos held steady while [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] placed Captain Crunch in the exact center—the fossil shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor, depending on the light. Around it, in a careful circle, he arranged the smooth stones from the jar, each one chosen for its shape or color or the way light moved through it. Forty-three treasures that the earth had given up and that he and Elena both understood how to see.

The light was extraordinary there—the last of the day catching the pale shell of the fossil and the smooth curves of the stones, turning them gold and then copper and then something that had no name. Looking at them, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could almost see the rooms where they had been found: the beach at Cadaques, the riverbed that rushed only in spring, the rocky shore of a place he had only heard described.

Below them, through the open door of the observatory, Bruno had circled three times and settled into the dust, his body warm and his eyes closed. The evening was settling toward its quiet. The first true stars were appearing, not the fading ghosts of them but the real lights that would remain through the whole night long.

Marcos stood beside [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO], not speaking, his hand resting on one of the wooden supports that held the treehouse steady. His walking stick remained on the ground far below, and for the moment he was simply present: an old man and a young boy, looking together at the things they had gathered, and at the sky opening above them like a door into a country they had only begun to know.

"Next time," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said quietly, "we will show her this."

Marcos nodded. He did not need to say yes twice. The treehouse held their answer in the light on the stones, in the dust where Bruno slept, in the stars that were coming out one by one, faithful and patient, the way they always did.

The other side of the hill was not a mystery anymore. But the world beyond it still had room for wonders.
